1.pericope_label: O come, let us sing unto the Lord: the joyful noise, the great King, and the deep places of the earth

schools.summary: Augustine hears a call to a banquet of joy and notes that the psalm distinguishes righteous joy from wicked by the addition of the words in the Lord.

Calvin takes the versions and the apostolic quotation as putting the authorship beyond doubt, presses the verb as meaning to make haste because we are naturally backward at thanksgiving, and locates the true worship in the sacrifice of praise rather than in ceremonies; Gill keeps the deep places to depths only God can penetrate.

Henry requires the body as well as the voice in worship and observes that we lack not matter for praise but heart; Spurgeon warns that much religious singing is offered to the ear of the congregation rather than to the Lord.

Clarke sets aside the apostolic ascription as following common opinion, dates the psalm to the captivity, reports its division into three speaking parts, reads the thanksgiving as a confession-offering, and distinguishes the three divine names of the third verse; Wesley keeps to the highest mountains.

Ellicott contrasts the general invitation with the heathen exclusion of the uninitiated and works the rare word for strength through two derivations; Keil and Delitzsch mark a second stanza beginning inside the seventh verse where God own voice answers, and reject the mining sense of the same word.

debates: Who wrote the psalm? Calvin holds that although the inscription is wanting, the ancient versions and the apostle who quotes it ascribe it to David, so that there can be no doubt; Clarke lists the same evidence and sets it aside, holding with eminent critics that the psalm was composed during the captivity and that the apostle only followed the common opinion, since the Psalter in general was attributed to David, and adding that nine manuscripts join the psalm to the one before although the subject is widely different.

What is the strength of the hills? Ellicott notes that the word is rare and that its usual root means to be weary, so that strength can be got from it only by deriving a word from its opposite, and offers either mines and treasures, from the labour of extraction, or, with the old versions, heights and sunny summits, which preserves an antithetic parallelism; Keil and Delitzsch reject the mining sense precisely because the clause must answer antithetically to the shafts of the earth, and deny that the derivation from weariness will serve at all.
outliers: Gill supports the singing of psalms to Christ from the letter of Pliny to Trajan, which reports that the Christians of that time sang a hymn to Christ as to a God.

Ellicott declines to explain away the reality granted to the tribal deities in the phrase King above all gods, asking how else Israel could have been constantly falling into the sin of worshipping them, and locating the preservation of the religion in the inspired refusal to allow them any sovereign power.
themes: a King above all rival powers
depths and heights alike in his hand
a divine voice breaking into the hymn

6.pericope_label: O come, let us worship and bow down: the sheep of his hand and the voice heard today

schools.summary: Henry marks that the latter part of the psalm begins in the middle of a verse, reports the reading that makes the clause a wish, identifies hearing the voice with believing, and lays the hardening wholly at the sinner own door; Spurgeon allows posture its place without making it everything and finds the master reason for worship in the covenant.
Gill requires an internal worship answering the external, in the exercise of every grace, and makes the possession run both ways between the shepherd and the flock.

Clarke distinguishes three acts in the three verbs of worship, would begin a new verse at the clause about hearing since it opens the part of the priest or prophet, presses the urgency of today, and notes the versions that divide the clause about the pasture otherwise; Wesley glosses today as forthwith.

Ellicott keeps the clause with the preceding half verse against the old Greek and the received version, arguing that a change of person within one sentence would be intolerable, and renders it as a wish; Keil and Delitzsch argue that the verb means to hear obediently so that no condition is possible, and answer an expositor who supplies a promised blessing.

debates: Where does the psalm turn, and how is the clause about hearing to be construed? Henry says the latter part begins in the middle of a verse and reports a reading that makes the clause a wish rather than a condition; Clarke would open a new verse there, since it begins the part of the priest or prophet; Keil and Delitzsch argue that the verb means to hear obediently so that the clause cannot be a protasis at all, and reject an apodosis supplied by another expositor in favour of an optative sense; Ellicott alone keeps the clause with the preceding half verse, holding the change of person within one sentence intolerable and requiring no lost line.

What do the three verbs of worship require? Clarke separates them into prostration, crouching and kneeling as three distinct acts; Ellicott takes the first as prostration and notes that kneeling low is reserved in the east for deep humiliation; Spurgeon holds that posture is not everything though it is something, since prayer is heard when knees cannot bend; Gill requires an inward worship to match the outward.
outliers: Clarke likens the second act of worship to a dog crouching with legs bent under in the presence of his master, waiting solicitously to receive his commands.
Ellicott observes that kneeling low is used in the east only in moments of deep humiliation, and notes how late in the history the practice is first mentioned.
themes: worship offered in body and in spirit
a covenant as the ground of praise
a flock led by a voice
a psalm interrupted by God own speech

8.pericope_label: Harden not your heart: the provocation in the wilderness and the rest they did not enter

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes four kinds of hardness of heart, finds loathing and weariness in the word rendered grieved, reports an older commentator who dates the displeasure from the affair of the spies, and attends to the form of the oath sworn by God upon himself.

Clarke takes the verb to know as expressing approbation, so that the fathers knew the ways well enough and would not walk in them, quotes his old Psalter on the same verse, holds the land to be a type of heaven, and notes how seldom the deserved judgment fell; Wesley reads the not knowing as a failure to consider, and keeps the rest to the promised land.

Ellicott marks the change of speaker at this verse, keeps the place names as proper names, renders the fathers a people of wanderers astray through ignorance, corrects grieved to loathed, and holds the rest to be plainly the promised land while describing the epistle use of the passage as a freedom of a kind the Jewish doctors ordinarily took.

debates: What is the rest they were not to enter? Ellicott holds it is of course the promised land, as the context unmistakably shows, and describes the application of the passage to a future rest in the epistle as a freedom of a kind the Jewish doctors ordinarily used; Clarke takes the land as a type of heaven where the faithful servant enters into the joy of his Lord; Wesley keeps it to the promised land; Gill turns rather to the oath and its form.

Did the fathers know God ways or not? Clarke argues that the verb expresses approbation, so that they knew his ways well enough but did not like them and would not walk in them; Ellicott renders them a people of wanderers in heart, morally astray through ignorance of God paths; Wesley says that after all the teaching given them they did not know nor consider the great things wrought for them.
outliers: Ellicott describes the use made of this passage by the author of the epistle, in order to make the psalm point to a future rest, as a freedom with the text of the kind the Jewish doctors ordinarily took.

Clarke gives his old Psalter on the erring generation, that these wretched men were given to the love of this life and knew not God ways of meekness and charity, wherefore in his wrath he set it stably that they should not enter into his rest.
themes: hardness of heart in several kinds
a place remembered by two names
